extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate mathematics students studying multivariable calculus and ODE theory
extracted.subtask_description: Statements, hypotheses, and proof ingredients for local existence and uniqueness of solutions to first-order ODE systems (Picard–Lindelöf, Cauchy–Peano) plus related prerequisites (Lipschitz condition, bounds) and techniques (Picard iteration, conversion to integral equation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for smoothness / normals for surface area
rubrics_metrics.description: For this reason the area of a bounding surface in R3 is defined by taking advantage of the direction perpendicular to the surface, and good behavior of the surface becomes essential. The notion of a 'normal' to the surface is then available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains that attempts to define surface area by inscribed polygons fail because there is no canonical projection; to make perpendicularity available one works with smooth manifolds-with-boundary (so normals exist). This motivates restricting to sufficiently regular (smooth) surfaces when defining surface area and applying higher-dimensional integral theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of Stokes's Theorem (generalized Green)
rubrics_metrics.description: Green’s Theorem in the plane admits a generalization for smooth manifolds-with-boundary of dimension k in Rn for every pair (k,n) with 2 ≤ k ≤ n. The result is that an integral on the boundary 'surface' is related to a 'volume' integral over the set. The results of this kind are collectively known as Stokes’s Theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The criterion for applying the general Stokes framework is smoothness of the manifold-with-boundary (availability of normals and suitable charts). Classical results (Green's, Stokes', Divergence/Gauss) fit into this framework when hypotheses on smoothness and dimensions are satisfied. The reader is referred to Spivak for full details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inscribed polygons need not give surface area
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus surface area cannot be defined by using inscribed polygons. The example shows sums of areas of inscribed triangles can be unbounded despite intuition from curves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an anti-pattern: attempting to define surface area by straightforward generalization of curve-length methods (inscribing polygons) fails. The text explains where intuition breaks down and why perpendicularity (normals) is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picard–Lindelöf (local existence) hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Let D be a nonempty open set in R1 × Cn, let (t0,y0) be in D, and suppose that F : D → Cn is a continuous function such that F(t,y) satisfies a Lipschitz condition in the y variable and |F(t,y)| ≤ M on a chosen compact rectangle R ⊂ D. Put a0 = min{a, b/M}. Then there exists a solution y(t) of the system y' = F(t,y) on the open interval |t − t0| < a0 satisfying the initial condition y(t0) = y0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theorem gives a precise local existence result under two concrete hypotheses: continuity of F and a Lipschitz condition in y (uniform in t on the compact region). The proof reduces the ODE to an integral equation and constructs successive approximations (Picard iterations), then uses the Weierstrass M-test for uniform convergence to obtain a continuous solution satisfying the integral (hence differential) equation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lipschitz condition ensures uniqueness
rubrics_metrics.description: If F : D → Cn satisfies a Lipschitz condition in the y variable on an open region D and (t0,y0) ∈ D, then there exists at most one solution y(t) to y' = F(t,y) on some neighborhood of t0 with y(t0) = y0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The uniqueness theorem (Theorem 4.2) is proved by applying the integral formulation and estimating differences between two candidate solutions using the Lipschitz constant to obtain bounds that force the difference to be zero. This is the standard route: Lipschitz in y ⇒ Grönwall-type control ⇒ uniqueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy–Peano existence (continuity suffices for local existence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A variant of Theorem 4.1 takes D ⊂ R1 × Cn and assumes only continuity of F (no Lipschitz). Then a local solution still exists (Cauchy–Peano theorem), but uniqueness need not hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook remarks that existence under mere continuity is provable (e.g., via Ascoli's Theorem) but uniqueness can fail (Example 5 in Section 1). Thus continuity alone is sufficient for existence but not for uniqueness; Lipschitz regularity in y is the extra hypothesis needed for uniqueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient condition for Lipschitz: bounded ∂F/∂y on compact convex sets
rubrics_metrics.description: If F is a real-valued continuous function of two real variables with a continuous partial derivative in the second variable, then the Mean Value Theorem gives F(t,y1) − F(t,y2) = (y1 − y2) ∂F/∂y(t,ξ) with ξ between y1 and y2. The partial derivative is bounded on any compact subset of D, and thus F satisfies, on any compact convex subset of D, a Lipschitz condition in the second variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical test: check boundedness of ∂F/∂y on the relevant compact (and convex) domain to obtain a Lipschitz constant. This is often how Lipschitz hypotheses are verified in applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picard iteration / integral equation technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Convert the differential equation y' = F(t,y) with y(t0)=y0 into the equivalent integral equation y(t) = y0 + ∫_{t0}^t F(s,y(s)) ds, then define successive approximations y_{n+1}(t) = y0 + ∫_{t0}^t F(s,y_n(s)) ds and show uniform convergence of the sequence (e.g., by Weierstrass M-test) to a continuous function y(t) which satisfies the integral equation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides both an existence proof and a constructive approximation scheme. The proof requires uniform bounds on F and the Lipschitz property to estimate differences and prove convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate structure in Picard proof (use of factorial decay)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Picard iteration proof one derives inductive estimates of the form |y_{n+1}(t) − y_n(t)| ≤ (M k^n / n!) |t−t0|^n on the chosen interval, which implies uniform convergence by comparison with the exponential series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These explicit bounds (involving (n!)^{-1}) are crucial to apply the Weierstrass M-test and establish uniform convergence of the Picard sequence; they also give error estimates for truncating the iteration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Converting higher-order ODEs to first-order systems
rubrics_metrics.description: A system of k equations of order m that has been solved for the mth-order derivatives is equivalent to a system of km equations of first order by introducing auxiliary variables (e.g., u1=y, u2=y').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduction is standard and allows treating higher-order scalar ODEs within the first-order system framework so that existence/uniqueness theorems apply uniformly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann–Stieltjes integral construction prerequisites
rubrics_metrics.description: Let α : [a,b] → R be a continuous nondecreasing function and f : [a,b] → R continuous. Define upper and lower sums U(P,f,α) and L(P,f,α) for partitions P by using sup and inf of f on subintervals multiplied by increments of α. If the upper and lower sums converge to a common limit as mesh → 0, that common limit is the Riemann–Stieltjes integral ∫_a^b f dα.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems 24–26 guide the student to show monotonicity of upper/lower sums under refinement, take inf/sup over partitions, control the difference via mesh size, and conclude existence of the integral for continuous f and continuous nondecreasing α. This supplies a precise step-by-step criterion for defining the Stieltjes integral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shoelace formula prerequisites and statement
rubrics_metrics.description: For any simple closed polygon whose m consecutive vertices are (x_j,y_j)_{j=1}^m, the area of the inside is Area = (1/2) Σ_{j=1}^m (x_j y_{j+1} − y_j x_{j+1}) (with indices cyclic, (x_{m+1},y_{m+1})=(x_1,y_1)). The absolute value signs are unnecessary if the polygon is traversed with the inside always on the left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This derives from combining Green's Theorem with a parametrization of polygonal boundary (Problems 27 & 32). Conditions: polygon must be simple (no self-intersections) and vertices listed in order. The formula is historically useful in surveying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourier-series criterion for harmonicity in unit disk
rubrics_metrics.description: If (c_n)_{n∈Z} is a doubly infinite sequence and for each r with 0≤r<1 the series Σ_{n=−∞}^∞ c_n r^{|n|} converges absolutely, then the corresponding Fourier series defines a C^∞ function in the open unit disk which is harmonic there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 14 shows how absolute convergence of the radial Fourier series for each r<1 ensures smoothness and harmonicity inside the disk. This gives a practical sufficient condition for constructing harmonic functions from Fourier coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arc length in polar coordinates formula (applicability)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a parametrically defined curve is given in polar coordinates by r = r(θ), then the arc length of a simple arc r(θ) from θ1 to θ2 is ∫_{θ1}^{θ2} sqrt(r(θ)^2 + (dr/dθ)^2) dθ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 21 asks to show this formula; it provides the criterion and formula for computing arc length for curves given in polar form, assuming r and dr/dθ exist and the arc is simple on the interval.
